  - text: Your Airbnb competition isn't just other Airbnbs. 👀🏨
  - text: "Here's what many new short-term rental investors overlook:"
  - text: If you're investing in a 1, 2, or 3-bedroom property, you may be entering a highly competitive category.
  - text: And here's the twist...
  - text: You're not just competing with similar rental listings.
  - text: You're also competing with HOTELS.
  - text: Because smaller groups of travelers might book one or two hotel rooms instead.
  - text: That means finding a good rental market isn't enough.
  - text: You also need to understand whether your property type can stand out.
  - text: Before you invest, know who you're competing against.
  - text: 💾 SAVE this before choosing your next property.
  - text: 📲 SHARE it with someone starting an Airbnb business.

  - text: Instead of only accumulating investments, some real estate investors are building portfolios of assets designed to produce ongoing cash flow.
  - text: And here's the interesting part...

  - text: Owning properties still takes work, but technology is changing how that work gets done.

  - text: The house isn’t just where the group stays.
  - text: It can be the reason they book.
  - text: One of the biggest opportunities in premium group travel is differentiation. Large vacation homes already serve groups — but relatively few operators fully commit to making design part of the experience.
  - text: That creates a gap.
  - text: When guests want a premium group experience, the property itself can become part of what they’re willing to pay for.
  - text: That realization pushed the business toward larger, design-focused luxury homes.
  - text: Would you rather stay in a basic house in the perfect location — or an unforgettable house 15 minutes farther away?
  - text: Save this if you’re building in hospitality or STRs, share it with an operator, and drop your answer below.

  - time: 11w
  - text: Airbnb is no longer the only place your short term rental makes money.
  - text: Most hosts are running a one-channel business without realizing it. One listing. One platform. One pool of travelers.
  - text: "Meanwhile:"
  - text: → Vrbo pulls families and groups booking longer stays
  - text: → Booking.com and Expedia now list whole single family homes — putting your property in front of travelers who never open Airbnb
  - text: → Google Travel added vacation rentals right next to Flights and Hotels
  - text: That last one matters most. Your property can now show up while someone is still planning the trip, before they've picked a booking site at all.
  - text: "Here's the uncomfortable part: if your revenue is flat, it's usually not the property. It's not the photos. It's not even the pricing."
  - text: It's that only one audience can see it.
  - text: Distribution is the cheapest lever in this entire business. No renovation. No new acquisition. No extra capital.
  - text: How many platforms are you currently listed on? Comment the number 👇

  - text: Groups pay $2,000 a night for the right Airbnb. And in the best markets, competition is shrinking.
  - text: Everyone keeps saying Airbnb is saturated.
  - text: Here's what we're seeing instead.
  - text: The markets where large groups pay $500, $1,000, even $2,000+ per night are the same markets where our clients have performed best over the years.
  - text: And across most of the markets we've done deals in, the competition is dropping.
  - text: "\"Saturated\" is the headline. The premium markets are telling a different story."
  - text: Always check current supply in your own market before you buy.
  - text: Is Airbnb saturated, or are people looking in the wrong markets? Comment below 👇

  - text: A great Airbnb market doesn’t need to win on every metric.
  - text: "We’re usually looking for a combination:"
  - text: High guest demand.
  - text: Less competition.
  - text: Attractive property economics.
  - text: But markets rarely give you everything.
  - text: Austin can have expensive land.
  - text: Waterfront areas in Florida can have expensive land.
  - text: That doesn’t automatically make them bad investments.
  - text: Sometimes the thing you lose in one category gets offset by stronger demand or better cash flow.
  - text: That’s the mistake with evaluating STR markets using one number.
  - text: You’re not looking for a “perfect” market.
  - text: You’re looking for the strongest overall tradeoff.
  - text: Save this before researching your next market.
  - text: Would you rather have stronger cash flow or better tax efficiency?
  - text: Share this with someone looking for their next STR market and follow for more real estate investing breakdowns.

  - time: 15w
  - text: A property can net $60,000 a year and I'll still tell you not to buy it.
  - text: Here's what new short term rental investors miss.
  - text: They look at the income. $20K, $40K, sometimes $60K a year in a strong market. Looks incredible on a spreadsheet.
  - text: Then you run the cash on cash return and it comes back at 8%. Sometimes 9%. Occasionally it scrapes 10%.
  - text: My repeat buyers — the ones who've closed deal after deal — won't touch it. Not because the income is bad. Because their capital can work harder somewhere else.
  - text: That's why those listings sit on the market for months while first-time buyers fight over them.
  - text: The floor is 10% to 12% cash on cash. Below it, you're not buying a deal. You're buying a job with a mortgage attached.
  - text: Income tells you what the property makes.
  - text: Cash on cash tells you what YOUR money makes.
  - text: Only one of those matters at the closing table.
  - text: What's your minimum cash on cash? Drop it below 👇

  - time: 12w
  - text: Doing the build-out yourself saves you 5 to 15 percent. That's it.
  - text: That number surprises people. Most investors assume running their own designer, their own GC, and their own furnishing process is where the real margin lives, so they commit to one path before they've priced the other one.
  - text: "Here's the move nobody makes: don't choose."
  - text: Get the local designers, the local property management teams, and the local GC crews to put a number on the scope. Then have your own team price the exact same scope. Two bids, same property, side by side.
  - text: Then you decide.
  - text: You keep full control of the decision. You get pricing pressure on both sides. And you find out fast which crew actually understands short term rentals and which one is quoting a normal remodel.
  - text: The investors who lose money on build-outs aren't the ones who picked wrong. They're the ones who only ever saw one number.
  - text: Which side won on your last build? Tell me below 👇
